title: Knowledge Check 11 - Lessons 51-55
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 51-55 - Data Mappers | Best Fit Solutions. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: A consultant is designing a Data Mapper that reads related records in one call. Which best practice applies?
options: Use a relationship query in an Extract
Read each record separately
Use a Load to read
Map every field on the object
questions.explanation: A relationship query reads related data in one call, reducing queries. Reading separately adds reads, a Load writes, and mapping every field wastes resources.

questions.question: A Data Mapper is used in multiple places in an integration. What is the best practice?
options: Duplicate it in each place
Reuse the single Data Mapper
Rename it for each use
Convert it to a Load
questions.explanation: Reusing a single Data Mapper keeps behavior consistent and reduces maintenance. Duplicating creates drift, renaming does not help, and converting to a Load changes the operation.

questions.question: A consultant is building a Load and must decide between insert, update, and upsert. What should guide the choice?
options: The number of fields
The business need for the write
The Data Mapper name
The output structure
questions.explanation: The business need determines whether records are created, updated, or upserted. Field count, name, and output structure do not drive the write operation.

questions.question: A flow reads source data, reshapes it, and writes it to Salesforce. What is the correct sequence of Data Mapper types?
options: Load, Transform, Extract
Extract or Turbo Extract, Transform, Load
Transform, Load, Extract
Load, Extract, Transform
questions.explanation: The flow reads with Extract or Turbo Extract, reshapes with Transform, and writes with Load. The other orders do not match the read, reshape, write sequence.

questions.question: In a write step of a flow, some records fail validation. What should the consultant have designed?
options: A branch that handles the failures
No error handling
A single Load with no output
A Transform after the Load
questions.explanation: Error handling branches on failures so the flow reacts gracefully. No handling leaves the data unknown, and the other options do not address the failures.

questions.question: A flow reads a large dataset but only a subset is needed. What best practice should the consultant apply to the read step?
options: Read all records and filter later
Filter in the query to read only what is needed
Use a Load to read
Map every field
questions.explanation: Filtering in the query reads only the needed records, keeping the read light. Reading all and filtering later wastes resources, and the other options do not reduce the read.

questions.question: An architect is asked to replace a Visualforce page that guides a user through a five-step application with a guided flow that reads and writes Salesforce records. Which recommendation is the best fit?
options: A custom Lightning Web Component with a state machine
An OmniScript with Data Mappers for the reads and writes
A FlexCard embedded on the record page
An Apex batch job that processes the application
questions.explanation: An OmniScript is purpose-built for guided, stateful user journeys and reads and writes records under the user's context, which matches the requirement. A Lightning Web Component would require hand-built state management and offers no advantage here. A FlexCard is for embedded display, not multi-step input. An Apex batch job is for background processing, not interactive guidance.

questions.question: A solution needs a read-only summary of a customer's open cases displayed on the account record page. The data is already in Salesforce. What is the best fit?
options: An OmniScript that queries the cases on load
An Integration Procedure called from a custom component
A FlexCard with a Data Raptor that reads the cases
A scheduled Apex job that writes the summary to a field
questions.explanation: A FlexCard is designed for embedded, read-only display and a Data Raptor reads the cases directly from Salesforce, which is the lightest correct fit. An OmniScript is overkill for a display-only widget. An Integration Procedure adds a server round trip for data that is already local. A scheduled job introduces staleness and extra writes for a read-only need.

questions.question: An OmniScript must display data whose source of truth is an external ERP. The architect must decide how the script gets that data. Which approach is the most defensible?
options: Have the OmniScript call the ERP directly on each step
Synchronize the needed ERP data into Salesforce and read it locally
Store the ERP data in a custom setting and read it from there
Ask the user to enter the ERP data manually in the script
questions.explanation: Synchronizing the needed data into Salesforce lets the OmniScript read local copies with predictable latency and failure handling, which is the defensible enterprise pattern. Calling the ERP on each step multiplies latency and failure points. A custom setting is for configuration, not transactional data. Manual entry is error-prone and defeats the purpose of integration.

questions.question: A team needs to move data from an external system into Salesforce as part of a nightly process. Which approach is the best fit?
options: An OmniScript that a user runs each night
An Integration Procedure invoked on a schedule
An Apex batch job or platform event driven integration
A FlexCard that displays the external data
questions.explanation: A scheduled, high-volume data load is a background integration, which belongs to Apex batch or platform events, not to user-facing OmniStudio components. An OmniScript requires a user to run it and is not built for volume. An Integration Procedure is request-response and not designed for scheduled bulk loads. A FlexCard only displays data and does not move it.

questions.question: The same external lookup is needed by three different OmniScripts. Where should the lookup logic live?
options: Duplicated inside each OmniScript
In a single shared Integration Procedure
In a custom setting that stores the response
In a FlexCard that each script embeds
questions.explanation: A shared Integration Procedure centralizes the external call and transformation so all three OmniScripts reuse one tested artifact. Duplicating the logic in each script creates drift and maintenance burden. A custom setting stores configuration, not a live lookup result. A FlexCard is a display component, not a service for OmniScripts to call.

questions.question: An architect is evaluating a guided multi-step claim intake flow that will be used by a small team of adjusters. What is the strongest reason to choose an OmniScript?
options: It is the only way to build a form in Salesforce
It runs faster than any other option at high volume
It provides a guided, stateful journey with built-in data handling under the user's context
It requires no security configuration because it bypasses sharing rules
questions.explanation: An OmniScript is purpose-built for guided, stateful journeys and handles data under the user's context, which matches a small-team claim intake. It is not the only way to build a form, so that reason is false. It is not optimized for high volume, so that reason is also false. It does not bypass sharing rules; it runs under them, so the last option is incorrect.

questions.question: An OmniScript feels slow on the first step even though the server is fast. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Add more Data Raptors to the first step so all data is ready
Defer data loading to the step that needs it and load only displayed fields
Increase the row limit on every Data Raptor
Move all logic into a single Integration Procedure
questions.explanation: Deferring data loading and loading only displayed fields reduces the work done on the first render, which is what the user perceives as slow. Adding more Data Raptors makes the first step slower. Increasing row limits returns more data and worsens the problem. Moving all logic into one IP does not address the load-time queries and may add a round trip.

questions.question: An Integration Procedure calls the same external system three times in a loop to gather data. What is the best optimization?
options: Keep the loop but add a longer timeout
Batch the calls into a single request and return only needed fields
Move the loop into the OmniScript
Cache the external system's entire database in Salesforce
questions.explanation: Batching the calls into a single request reduces round trips, and returning only needed fields keeps the payload small, which directly cuts latency. A longer timeout does not reduce the number of calls. Moving the loop into the OmniScript just relocates the problem to the browser. Caching the entire external database is not feasible or appropriate.

questions.question: A Data Raptor that filters on a non-indexed field is slow and returns thousands of rows. What is the correct fix?
options: Remove the filter so the query returns everything
Filter on an indexed field and add a row limit where the business allows
Run the query inside a loop to split the work
Convert the Data Raptor to a FlexCard
questions.explanation: Filtering on an indexed field makes the query selective, and a row limit bounds the result set, which addresses both the slowness and the row-count risk. Removing the filter returns even more rows. Running the query in a loop multiplies the queries and hits limits. A FlexCard is a display component and does not fix the query.
